metrics.label: Henry Hub gas

metrics.label: Baltic Capesize Index
metrics.blurb: The Capesize component of the Baltic Dry Index. The most volatile part, and effectively a bet on Chinese steel production.

metrics.label: Baltic Panamax Index
metrics.blurb: The Panamax component. Coal and grain rather than iron ore, so it follows harvests and power demand more than steel.

metrics.label: Baltic Supramax Index
metrics.blurb: The Supramax component. These ships have their own cranes and serve smaller ports, so it reflects broad trade rather than one commodity.

metrics.label: Baltic Dry Index

metrics.label: VLSFO Singapore

metrics.label: Diesel crack vs Brent

brief.text:
The clearest news in today's data is fuel. Bunker prices — the fuel ships burn, and usually the largest single voyage cost a charterer pays — fell across all four main ports this morning. VLSFO (very low sulphur fuel oil, the standard grade) was quoted at $907.50 a tonne in Fujairah, down $49.00 or 5.1%, and at $901.50 in Singapore, down $40.00 or 4.2%, with Rotterdam at $747.00 (-1.1%) and Houston at $764.00 (-2.1%). Cheaper bunkers lift the earnings an owner nets from the same freight rate, so it matters directly to anyone fixing a voyage today.

Crude also eased today: Brent, the global crude benchmark, is $93.98 a barrel, down 0.64 (-0.7%), and WTI, the US benchmark, is $86.99, down 1.13 (-1.3%), leaving the Brent–WTI spread at $6.99. Gasoil is $4.15 a gallon (-1.4%) and RBOB gasoline $2.70 (-0.9%); Henry Hub gas is $2.94/mmBtu (-0.5%). The diesel crack against Brent — refiners' margin on diesel — stands at $80.26 a barrel, with no change figure given. Nothing in today's headlines explains the fall in crude or bunkers; the data here does not show why. No freight benchmark has refreshed today. For background only: the Baltic Dry Index, which tracks dry bulk cargo rates, was 2,694 points on Wednesday 4 November, unchanged, with the Capesize index (largest bulkers, typically iron ore and coal) at 4,097 the same day. The tanker ETF BWET was $691.60 on Wednesday, down 17.2%, a large move the data does not explain.

Running stories: today's headlines add a sanctions development — the US sanctioned a network of fraudulent ship registries and false-flag services used by Iran's shadow fleet. The attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the Black Sea drone strikes, the Russian diesel export ban, the US West Coast port labour standoff and Gulf chokepoint congestion all had no fresh news today and are unchanged. Somali piracy also features, with an Iranian dhow hijacked on 29 October, the fourth hijacking off Somalia this year.

What to watch: whether the Baltic tanker and dry bulk indices refresh tomorrow, since the last tanker TCE prints — TCE meaning time charter equivalent, daily earnings on a voyage — date from 1 November or earlier. Also watch how the new registry sanctions affect which tonnage is acceptable for Gulf liftings.

storylines.title: Direct attacks on ships in Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have continued into November, including a VLCC whose engine room was struck in Omani waters, reported as the fifth confirmed attack in the first three days of the month.
storylines.why_it_matters: Strikes on hulls raise war-risk premiums and crew-safety objections for Arabian Gulf liftings, shrinking the pool of willing owners and supporting crude and product tanker earnings.

storylines.title: Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab transits and Gulf congestion
storylines.what: Strait of Hormuz traffic rose in October to its highest monthly level since July, supported by stronger dry bulk and LNG movements even as VLCC traffic declined. Red Sea traffic also rose. Vessel waiting remains elevated across the Arabian Gulf.
storylines.why_it_matters: Transit counts and waiting times show whether ships route through or around high-risk waters, changing voyage lengths, tonne-mile demand and effective fleet supply.
sources: LR Advisory launches Supply Chain Resilience service

storylines.title: US sanctions on Iran shadow-fleet registries
storylines.what: The United States sanctioned a network of individuals and companies accused of running fraudulent ship registries and false-flag services for Iranian shadow fleet vessels, alongside a new warning to the industry.
storylines.why_it_matters: Flag and registry fraud sanctions force charterers, insurers and class societies to re-check documentation, and can push sanctioned tonnage out of mainstream trades, tightening compliant tanker supply.

storylines.why_it_matters: Labour action at container and ferry berths disrupts berthing schedules and cargo flows, and the unresolved US West Coast dispute leaves a large share of US import capacity exposed to stoppage.
sources: Transpacific emerges as liner shipping's golden trade
